## "Write it down the way we'd write down a CAPA"

Four days after the eQMS (electronic quality-management system) go-live meeting, your Quality
Analyst catches you between calls with a question that isn't really a question. "I keep thinking
about what you said to [the systems administrator] — thirty days, report the results, clean or
not. Where does that actually live?" You point at the meeting minutes. She doesn't look
convinced. "Minutes get filed and forgotten. If this were a CAPA (corrective and preventive
action) finding, I'd have opened a tracked record the same day: the gap, the action, the owner,
the date, who signs off on closing it. Right now this is just a very well-worded sentence
someone said out loud."

She's right, and it's worth sitting with why. The authorization decision itself — module 4's
decision — was real. It had a name on it, a date, an explicit acceptance. But a decision and a
tracking record are two different things. A decision says "here's what we're doing about this."
A tracking record is what still exists in ninety days if the decision-maker is on vacation, the
systems administrator changes roles, or an AABB (Association for the Advancement of Blood &
Biotherapies) assessor asks to see it. NIST (the National Institute of Standards and Technology)
has a name for that tracking record in its own Risk Management Framework (RMF): a **POA&M** —
plan of action and milestones. Your QA, reaching for the closest thing she already trusts, called
it by its quality-system name instead: a CAPA. Both of you are pointing at the same gap in your
own process right now. This module closes it, and then asks the more interesting question: now
that you can build both, what's actually the same between them, and what genuinely isn't?

## Why this step exists — and the ITSM bridge

Here's the failure a POA&M and a CAPA both exist to prevent, and it's a close cousin of the one
module 4 already named, one step further down the line. Module 4 stopped a decision from
happening silently, by default, the day a go-live date arrived. This module stops something that
happens *after* a decision has already been made honestly: a named, accepted risk that quietly
stops being tracked, because the acceptance itself felt like the finish line. "I accepted it" is
not the same sentence as "and here's how Lakeshore knows, three months from now, whether the
thing I accepted ever actually got fixed."

You already run the ITSM (IT service management) version of this discipline, and — usefully — so
does your Quality Analyst, in a different vocabulary. Think about **problem management**: an
incident gets resolved, the immediate service is restored, but the underlying root cause can't be
permanently fixed today — maybe it needs a vendor patch, a budget cycle, a maintenance window.
A mature problem management practice doesn't just shrug and move on. It opens a **problem
record**, with a known error logged in the KEDB (known error database), a named owner, and a
target date for the permanent fix — tracked, visibly, until it actually closes. CAPA is that
exact discipline, aimed at a quality deviation instead of a service incident, which is precisely
the bridge `capa-root-cause-to-effectiveness` already built for you. **A POA&M is the identical
discipline a third time, aimed at a security or risk-control deficiency instead of either one.**
Three different originating worlds — ITIL, AABB's Quality System Essentials, NIST's RMF — all
landed on the same answer: a known gap needs a tracked record with an owner and a date, or it
isn't actually being managed. It's being tolerated.

## The rule in plain English

A POA&M entry does one job: it takes a deficiency someone already found — here, the one Assess
surfaced in module 3 and Authorize accepted in module 4 — and turns it into a tracked commitment.
Concretely, that means naming the specific gap, naming the specific action that closes it, naming
who owns that action, naming a date by which it has to be done, and naming who reviews the
progress and decides whether the commitment was actually met. Nothing about this is exotic. It's
the same five questions you'd ask about any open item on a project plan — what's wrong, what are
we doing about it, who's doing it, by when, and who checks. NIST's own version of this just
happens to have a name and a specific place in RMF's Authorize step where it lives.

One thing worth saying plainly, the same way this course has said it about every other borrowed
piece of RMF: nothing about a POA&M is a legal requirement for Lakeshore. No regulator audits
Lakeshore's POA&M log. Lakeshore is building this entry because it's a genuinely well-built
tracking instrument, the same reason it borrowed Categorize, Select, Implement, Assess, and
Authorize in the four modules before this one — not because anyone outranks Lakeshore into
using NIST's paperwork.

## Citation decoder

| Citation | How to read it aloud | What it requires | In our scenario |
|---|---|---|---|
| NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2, Ch. 3 (Authorize step, Task A-6 — plan of action and milestones) | "Special Publication eight-hundred-thirty-seven, Revision two, Chapter Three, Task A-six" | U.S. government work, public domain, safe to quote verbatim. Describes what a plan of action and milestones includes, who reviews it, and when an entry isn't even necessary. | The one new source this module draws on — the instrument you build below for the eQMS's open access-review item. |

That's the whole table. This module owns no new regulatory content beyond this single passage —
everything else here is synthesis of what modules 1 through 4 already built, plus one reference
to a CAPA module this course doesn't re-teach.

## The actual text

Quoted verbatim from `sources/nist/sp-800-37r2-excerpt.md` — the fullest, most load-bearing POA&M
passage the saved excerpt contains:

> The plan of action and milestones is included as part of the authorization package. The plan
> of action and milestones describes the actions that are planned to correct deficiencies in the
> controls identified during the assessment of the controls and during continuous monitoring. The
> plan of action and milestones includes tasks to be accomplished with a recommendation for
> completion before or after system authorization; resources required to accomplish the tasks;
> milestones established to meet the tasks; and the scheduled completion dates for the milestones
> and tasks. The plan of action and milestones is reviewed by the authorizing official to ensure
> there is agreement with the remediation actions planned to correct the identified deficiencies.
> It is subsequently used to monitor progress in completing the actions. Deficiencies are accepted
> by the authorizing official as residual risk or are remediated during the assessment or prior to
> submission of the authorization package to the authorizing official. Plan of action and
> milestones entries are not necessary when deficiencies are accepted by the authorizing official
> as residual risk.

Read it slowly, because almost every clause maps onto something you already have sitting on the
record from module 4.

**"Tasks to be accomplished with a recommendation for completion before or after system
authorization."** Lakeshore's eQMS access review wasn't completed before authorization — Option B
was authorizing now, with remediation scheduled *after*. That's not an irregular use of a POA&M;
it's exactly the "after" half of this clause, named explicitly.

**"Resources required to accomplish the tasks."** For this entry, modest and already real: the
systems administrator's own time to actually sit down and run the review against the eQMS's
current account list. No new budget line, no new tool, no new hire — the review mechanism itself
already exists from module 3's Implement step. The gap was never capability. It was simply that
the first cycle hadn't run yet.

**"Milestones... and the scheduled completion dates."** The 30-day window, named on the record in
module 4's own authorization language.

**"Reviewed by the authorizing official to ensure there is agreement with the remediation actions
planned."** That's you, the Director — the same accountable role Authorize already gave you, now
doing a second job: not just accepting the risk, but confirming the plan to close it is one you
actually agree with.

**"Subsequently used to monitor progress in completing the actions."** This is the thread that
connects straight back to Monitor's own one-line action, already quoted in `authorize-and-
monitor`. A POA&M isn't a one-time memo — it's the specific artifact Monitor checks against.

Now the sentence worth reading twice, because it's the one genuinely surprising line in this
whole passage: **"Plan of action and milestones entries are not necessary when deficiencies are
accepted by the authorizing official as residual risk."** Taken on its own, that could sound like
Lakeshore didn't need to build anything at all — you already accepted the risk in module 4, full
stop. That reading misses what actually happened in that room, and it's worth being precise about
the difference. A bare acceptance — "this is a known gap, and I'm choosing to live with it,
indefinitely, no further action planned" — is the case this sentence is describing, and that case
genuinely doesn't need a POA&M entry; there's nothing left to track. What you did in module 4 was
different in one specific, deliberate way: you accepted the risk **for a bounded window, tied to
a named remediation action with its own date.** That's not a bare acceptance. It's the "accepted,
with a recommendation for completion after authorization" case the earlier part of this same
passage describes — which is exactly the case a POA&M entry exists to track. The distinction is
honest and worth keeping straight: NIST's own text doesn't require Lakeshore to write this entry.
What it requires is that *if* Lakeshore's acceptance comes bundled with a planned action and a
date — which yours does — that's precisely the situation the instrument was built for.

## Lakeshore's own POA&M entry

Here's the entry itself, built from the exact facts module 4 already put on the record, nothing
invented:

| Field | This entry |
|---|---|
| **Finding / deficiency** | The quarterly eQMS access-review control (account and identity management) is implemented and documented, but has not yet been exercised on its first scheduled cycle. |
| **Planned action** | Run the first quarterly access review against the eQMS's current account list, across all three sites, and report the results. |
| **Resources required** | The systems administrator's own time; the review mechanism already exists from Implement — no new tool, budget, or staffing. |
| **Recommendation for completion** | After authorization — the Director authorized the eQMS for production now, with this action scheduled to follow, not a precondition to go-live. |
| **Owner** | The systems administrator. |
| **Milestone / scheduled completion date** | Within 30 days of the Director's authorization decision. |
| **Reviewed and accepted by** | The Director, as Lakeshore's own authorizing official. |
| **Status / closure rule** | A clean result closes the acceptance. A finding (a stale account, a mismatched role) becomes a new, immediate finding on its own record — not something this entry already waived. If the 30-day date passes with no review run, the authorization itself is reopened, per module 4's own standing trigger. |

That's it. There's nothing in this table that wasn't already said out loud in module 4's own
authorization sentence — the only thing this module adds is the discipline of writing it down in
a form that survives a staff change, a long weekend, or an assessor's question six months from
now, instead of living only in a meeting transcript.

## Placing it next to a CAPA

Your Quality Analyst's instinct — "if this were a CAPA, I'd already have a tracked record" — was
exactly right, and it's worth saying precisely why, instead of just agreeing. `quality-system-
essentials`'s own CAPA module, `capa-root-cause-to-effectiveness`, already built the full
mechanics of a CAPA in depth: root cause analysis past the first "why," a corrective action for
the instance found, a preventive action for the systemic cause, and a required effectiveness check
with its own pre-agreed criterion, time window, data source, and failure definition. This module
doesn't re-teach any of that. What it does is put the finished POA&M table above right next to
that structure and ask, honestly, where they match and where they don't.

**Where they genuinely match.** Both instruments exist for the identical underlying reason: a
known gap doesn't get to just sit there unnamed. Both require a root finding, a planned action, a
named owner, a milestone date, and review by someone with real authority to accept or reject the
plan — the authorizing official for a POA&M, whoever signs CAPA closure for a quality deviation.
Both come from completely different originating worlds — NIST's RMF, built for federal
information security; AABB's Quality System Essentials, built for regulated biologics quality —
and arrived at the same shape of answer anyway. That convergence is the real teaching point of
this entire course, not a coincidence: a prioritized, dated, owned remediation record for a known
gap is simply what a mature risk-management process looks like, regardless of which regulatory
family invented the vocabulary for it.

**Where they genuinely differ, and it's worth being honest about this rather than flattening it.**
Re-read Task A-6's own text above carefully: nowhere does it ask for a documented root-cause
analysis before the planned action, and nowhere does it require a formal, pre-agreed effectiveness
check after the fix, the way CAPA's own structure explicitly does. A POA&M entry's own closing
language is simply "used to monitor progress in completing the actions" — progress against a
schedule, not a required, independently verified proof that the fix actually worked, checked
against a criterion written down in advance. RMF's separate Monitor step (already quoted in
`authorize-and-monitor`) does include "assessing control effectiveness" as an ongoing, standing
obligation — so effectiveness isn't absent from RMF altogether. It just isn't built into the
POA&M instrument itself the way it's built directly into CAPA's own four-stage structure, with its
own named, required final stage.

| | POA&M (NIST RMF, Task A-6) | CAPA (AABB QSE 9) |
|---|---|---|
| Root finding | A control deficiency, from assessment or monitoring | A deviation or nonconformance, from investigation |
| Root-cause analysis required by the text itself | Not specified — the deficiency is treated as already named | Explicit and central — must go past the first "why" to a systemic cause |
| Planned action | Tasks, resources, milestones, scheduled completion dates | Corrective action (the instance) and preventive action (the system) |
| Owner | Named individual accomplishing the tasks | Named individual(s) for each action |
| Review/acceptance authority | The authorizing official | Whoever signs CAPA closure |
| Verification after the fix | "Monitor progress" — schedule tracking; effectiveness lives in RMF's separate Monitor step, not inside Task A-6 itself | A required effectiveness check: pre-agreed criterion, time window, data source, defined failure condition |
| Entry required even for a bare, indefinite acceptance | No — Task A-6 says so directly | Yes — a reported deviation doesn't have a "just accept it, no record" option |

Here's the honest reason this particular entry doesn't make the difference feel sharper than it
is. The access-review gap has an unusually obvious root cause — the review simply hadn't run yet
on schedule — so skipping a formal root-cause step costs nothing this time. That won't always be
true. A future POA&M entry, for a genuinely unclear deficiency, would benefit from borrowing
CAPA's root-cause discipline even though Task A-6's own text doesn't demand it — the same way this
course has already shown Lakeshore borrowing structure voluntarily when it's simply a better way
to work, not because any instrument requires it. Say that to your CIO exactly this plainly: a
POA&M and a CAPA are the same motion in two vocabularies, with one real difference in emphasis
worth naming rather than glossing over.

## What a reviewer would actually look for

What a competent reviewer wants — your CIO, an AABB assessor who happens to ask about the eQMS
during a future reassessment, or you yourself revisiting this in six months — is the table above,
not the meeting minutes it was built from. A bad answer sounds like "we talked about it and the
systems administrator was going to handle it." A good answer produces a dated entry with a named
owner, a specific date, and a closure rule that was written down *before* the 30 days ran out, not
reconstructed afterward depending on how the review happened to turn out.

## Common traps

**"The Director already accepted the risk in module 4, so writing a POA&M entry now is
redundant."** Not quite, and the distinction matters. A bare, indefinite acceptance genuinely
wouldn't need one, per Task A-6's own words. This acceptance came with a named action and a date
attached — which is exactly the situation the instrument exists to track. The entry doesn't
duplicate the authorization decision; it's what keeps that decision from quietly becoming a bare
acceptance by default, the same way an unwritten authorization becomes a shrug.

**"A POA&M and a CAPA are literally the same form, just with different labels on the boxes."**
Also not quite. The overlap is real and is this module's whole point — finding, action, owner,
date, review. But CAPA's own text demands a documented root-cause chain and a formal, pre-agreed
effectiveness check; Task A-6's own text asks for neither inside the POA&M instrument itself.
Calling them identical erases a real difference in what each one requires you to prove before you
get to call the gap closed.

## What this means for your job

- **Treat an accepted risk with a remediation date as an open tracking item, not a closed
  conversation.** The acceptance and the tracking record are two different artifacts; only one of
  them survives a staff change.
- **Ask, for any gap someone wants to "just accept," whether a real action and date are attached.**
  If yes, write the entry — that's exactly the case Task A-6 describes. If genuinely no further
  action is planned, say that honestly instead of building a hollow tracking record for a decision
  that was always a flat acceptance.
- **When you compare a POA&M to a CAPA for your CIO or your QA, name the real difference, not just
  the real overlap.** Both track remediation to a date with a named owner. CAPA additionally
  demands root cause and a verified effectiveness check; a bare POA&M entry does not, by NIST's
  own text, though nothing stops Lakeshore from borrowing that discipline anyway when a deficiency
  is genuinely unclear.
- **Never let "we accepted it" stand in for "and here's how we'll know it's actually fixed."**
  That gap is exactly what your QA caught four days after the go-live meeting, and it's the
  instinct worth keeping for every future accepted risk, security or quality.
- **Hold the closure rule to the standard you already set in module 4.** A clean review closes
  this specific entry. A finding opens a new one. The 30-day date passing with nothing run reopens
  the authorization itself — not a quiet extension nobody wrote down.

## Check your understanding

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q1: Your systems administrator says, "The Director already accepted this risk — why do we need to write a separate POA&M entry at all?" Is he right that NIST's own text requires one here?

Not quite, and the honest answer has two parts. NIST's own text says plainly that POA&M entries
"are not necessary when deficiencies are accepted by the authorizing official as residual risk" —
so a flat, indefinite acceptance genuinely wouldn't need one. But that's not what happened in
module 4. The Director's acceptance came bundled with a named action (the first access review)
and a specific date (30 days) — which is exactly the "recommendation for completion... after
system authorization" case the same passage describes as needing tasks, resources, milestones,
and a scheduled date tracked. The entry isn't an NIST mandate standing on its own; it's the right
instrument for the specific kind of acceptance Lakeshore actually made.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q2: Your Quality Analyst asks whether this POA&M entry needs a documented root-cause analysis and a scheduled effectiveness check, the way one of her CAPAs would. Does it?

Not by NIST's own text. Task A-6's POA&M passage asks for tasks, resources, milestones, and
scheduled completion dates, reviewed by the authorizing official and then used to "monitor
progress in completing the actions" — it never asks for a documented root-cause chain or a formal,
pre-agreed effectiveness criterion the way CAPA's own four-stage structure explicitly does. In
this case the root cause is close to self-evident (the review simply hadn't run on schedule), so
skipping that step costs little. A genuinely unclear deficiency would be a good candidate for
borrowing CAPA's root-cause discipline voluntarily — a sensible practice, not something the POA&M
instrument itself demands.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q3: The systems administrator runs the review on day 28 and finds one stale account that should have been removed weeks earlier. Does that mean this POA&M entry failed?

No — read the closure rule again, the same one module 4 built: a clean result closes the
acceptance; a finding becomes a new, immediate finding of its own, not something this entry
already waived. Finding the stale account inside the 30-day window is the process working exactly
as designed — the whole reason the review existed was to catch exactly this kind of drift. What
would actually be a failure is the 30-day date passing with no review run at all, and nobody
noticing.
:::

## Where this course ends, and what's still ahead

Five modules ago, this course opened with two competent people — your Quality Analyst, fluent in
ICH Q9; your systems administrator, running real but undocumented risk judgment — having two
disconnected risk conversations about the same new system. It closes today with both of those
conversations finally sharing one vocabulary, and a tracked record to prove it.

Here's the arc, named once, start to finish. Module 1 put NIST's Risk Management Framework, ISO
31000, and ICH Q9(R1) side by side and showed they run the identical six-part motion —
identify, respond, implement, verify, accept, monitor — in three vocabularies from three very
different kinds of body, and chose RMF's structure, voluntarily, as the one worth running for the
eQMS end to end. Module 2 applied RMF's own Categorize and Select steps to the eQMS itself:
reasoned it to moderate-impact, and selected a tailored set of control families — account and
identity management, audit/logging, physical and environmental protection — sized to that
impact, not copied from a template built for a smaller system. Module 3 built those three control
families for real, then handed the assessment to someone who hadn't built them, applying this
curriculum's own auditor-independence principle — and found the one honest gap this course has
carried ever since: a quarterly access-review control, implemented and documented, not yet
exercised on its first scheduled cycle. Module 4 put a name and a date on what to do about that
gap: the Director authorized the eQMS for production now, across all three sites, explicitly
accepting that one deficiency as a named, time-bound residual risk, with a 30-day remediation
commitment — and delivered this course's single load-bearing sentence, that authorizing a system
this way is the same underlying motion as a validation release followed by periodic review. And
this module took that exact commitment and gave it the tracked record it was always missing: a
real POA&M entry, built field by field from facts module 4 had already put on the record, placed
next to a CAPA to show the same motion in a second vocabulary — genuinely alike in finding, action,
owner, date, and review; genuinely different in how hard each one leans on root-cause depth and a
formal effectiveness check.

Say plainly what this course leaves you with, because it's the whole point of having built it.
Lakeshore now has one shared vocabulary for a sentence you'll need constantly, in every room you
sit in: *here's a known gap, here's the plan, here's the date, here's who signed off on it* —
whether the gap surfaced as a security control deficiency tracked on a POA&M or a quality
deviation tracked on a CAPA. That sentence doesn't change shape depending on which regulatory
family is in the room. Neither should your confidence saying it.

Two courses in this curriculum's Track 4 pick this vocabulary back up directly.
`healthcare-security-and-privacy` will run HIPAA (Health Insurance Portability and Accountability
Act) breach response and privacy-control gaps through the same RMF-shaped reasoning this course
just built — categorizing what a privacy failure would cost, selecting safeguards sized to that,
and tracking whatever's left on exactly this same kind of entry.
`vendor-and-third-party-risk-management` will turn this course's own scrutiny outward, onto every
vendor underneath Lakeshore's systems — reading a vendor's own risk posture, tiering it, and
tracking a vendor's open gaps the identical way you just tracked the eQMS's. And Track 5's
capstone, `itsm-for-regulated-blood-services`, is where this risk vocabulary finally sits next to
ITIL's own problem management and continual improvement practices in one crosswalk, in language
built to survive a conversation with your CIO and your exec quality council in the same breath.

You came into this course running two separate, competent risk conversations with no shared
floor under either one. You leave it able to take any system through categorize, select,
implement, assess, authorize, and monitor, and track whatever's left over on a record that holds
up in any room you carry it into — security, quality, or your own CIO's.
